messages.author: 959bffbdb3ddae02
messages.subject: SPDE and pseudo-absences
parts:
Dear R-INLA people,

I hope you can help me. I am using INLA to fit a Log Gaussian Cox Process with the SPDE method. I have data of observed animals locations (coded with 1) and pseudo-absences (coded with 0).

The classical SPDE method goes as follows:
1) The observed locations are coded with 1.
2) Create a mesh where the nodes are coded with a 0 and the environmental covariates at the nodes are needed.
3) Create weigths based on the voronoi polygons.
4) Project the mesh to the observed locations
5) Fit the model.

I have found one paper about Species Distribution Modelling (https://besjournals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/2041-210X.12352) where they have observed locations (coded with 1) and pseudo-absences (coded with 0) and they use the INLA-SPDE method to fit their model which goes as follows:

1) The observed locations are coded with 1, the pseudo-absences are coded with 0
2) Create a uniform mesh
3) Project the mesh to the observed locations AND TO THE PSEUDO-ABSENCES
4) The covariates are specified at the observed locations and at the pseudo-absences locations BUT NOT AT THE MESH NODES.
5) The weigths are not based on the voronoi polygons. They are specified as constant weights (spatial_resolution^2)
6) Fit the model

Similar to the mesh nodes, the pseudo-absences are integration points. Thus, Ideally I would like to specify a mesh which nodes are located exactly at the locations of the pseudo-absences and then use the classical SPDE method. However, this leads to completely wrong results. Thus, I have the following questions:

a) Are these pseudo-absences different integration points than the mesh nodes? If no, why is my model leading to wrong results?

b) Is the method presented in the paper also valid if I have pseudo-absences which are not uniformly located in the study area?

c) Is it still possible to use weigths based on the voronoi polygons? If so, how?

Thank you very much and have a nice day!

Best regards,

Rafael

messages.author: afb003e064114795
messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] SPDE and pseudo-absences
parts:
Hi Rafael,

this is a good question that often comes up for presence-only data, and the answer is a bit complex, and depends on precisely how the "pseudo-absences" are constructed/chosen/invented.

1) If both presences and absences were observed at specific locations, then the natural observation model would be a Bernoulli model at those locations (Bin(1,p))
2) If the presences were obtained through complete search of a region (optionally with imperfect but model-able detection probability) then the natural model
would be a Log Gaussian Cox process, where the likelihood involves a sum over the log-intensity at the presences, and subtracting the integral of the intensity over the entire region.

For case 2, we can implement that for mesh based spde predictors by using a numerical integration scheme. In order for the resulting likelihood approximation to be stable,
the integration scheme must not fail to counterbalance the sum in the likelihood. Such failure can lead it to estimate infinite intensity at the absences, and zero intensity elsewhere.
For this reason, the safest integration scheme is one that places integration points at all mesh nodes, since that "surrounds" any possible presence, and ensures the likelihood doesn't degenerate.
In case the mesh is chosen to have mesh nodes coinciding with presences, one could conceivably be a bit more flexible as long as one also has integration points at those nodes, but that mostly
leads to the same integration points; placing them at the mesh nodes.

In this general LGCP approximation, one may use the voronoi cells around each mesh node as integration point, but that's a 0-order approximation of the integral (i.e. piecewise constant intensity around each mesh node). If we instead build an integration scheme based on the basis functions in the mesh, we get a higher order approximation of the continuous domain model. Both are valid approaches, but the automated implementation in the inlabru interface lgcp() function uses the higher order approximation.

Now we get to the presence-only case:
3) If we only have presences, but for some reason an LGCP is _not_ the natural true model, but we invent pseudo-absences in order to mimic the LGCP likelihood discussed above.
However, unless the pseudo-absences and associated weights are chosen appropriately, it may not be a valid likelihood model.
(Note: it's not always clear to me when this is appropriate; for cases where an actual LGCP _is_ the appropriate model, one should go back to the fundamentals and not prematurely invent pseudo-absences. And when an LGCP is _not_ the appropriate model, then the entire construction relies on the pseudo-absences&weights _defining_ an appropriate model structure.)

The problem is that _if_ the intensity field is determined only by large scale covariates that vary slowly over space, then the pseudo-absences and related weights can provide a stable likelihood expression, since changing the covariate weights affects the whole field, and the degenerate case discussed above will typically not happen. But when we introduce a Gaussian field into the log-intensity, that's no longer the case, and all the issues discussed above return.
In the paper you linked, they appear to get around the issue by always including the presence locations as pseudo-absences (see eqn 5, where the presences are included in the integral approximation).
Thus, as mentioned above for integration points coinciding with mesh nodes, if they choose the weights appropriately, this can yield a valid stable likelihood expression, and just need enough integration points to resolve the needed spatial scales of the Gaussian field.
How appropriate such a model is depends on the application and how the weights are chosen.

But in all the cases above, the covariates need to be available for every location where there is either an observation or an integration point.
So if you make an integration scheme that doesn't include the mesh nodes, that should be ok, _if_ the other requirements on a stable likelihood model are fulfilled, as discussed above.

The main issues seem to be 
1) how to choose the pseudo-absence weights for the presence locations, and
2) how to choose the pseudo-absence weights for the other pseudo-absence integration points.

I couldn't immediately see how they differentiate between those two types of points when choosing the weights, but the reason for constant weights seems to be that they used a uniform grid of integration points, in which case the grid cells _are_ the voronoi sets. However, that doesn't quite work if the presence locations also need integration weights. If they set those to zero, then they only get a stable integration scheme if it's dense enough in space.

In summary, the issues are that
1) presence-only data doesn't necessarily have a well-defined observation likelihood model 
2) _If_ one assumes it can be modelled with an LGCP model, one needs to ensure a stable likelihood approximation, and "pseudo-absence" is just a fancy word for "location of a point in a numerical integration scheme", and going back to how to construct valid integral approximations provides solutions to the problem.
3) Such an approximation may be more or less appropriate, depending on how the weights at presences are chosen, and how the weights at pseudo-absences are chosen (including cases that are specifically _not_ approximations of a well-defined LGCP, but instead a model solely _defined_ by the pseudo-absences and weights).

Related references that discuss the case when an LGCP _is_ the model, but not the special presence-only situation:
https://academic.oup.com/biomet/article/103/1/49/2389990
https://projecteuclid.org/journals/annals-of-applied-statistics/volume-11/issue-4/Point-process-models-for-spatio-temporal-distance-sampling-data-from/10.1214/17-AOAS1078.full

Best wishes,
Finn

Dear Prof. Dr. Lindgren,

thank you for such a great explanation!

Regarding the paper I posted here, they show in their appendix the implementation. For the observed locations they use zero weights. Can I use here weights based on the areas of the voronoi polygons of the pseudo-absences (NOT OF THE MESH NODES)? 

Thank you

Best regards

Rafael

messages.author: afb003e064114795
messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] SPDE and pseudo-absences
parts:
Hi,

for “strategically placed pseudo-absences”, the problem is that it doesn’t guarantee a stable integration scheme for the likelihood.  For known/fixed intensity, using the voronoi cell areas would be a valid integral approximation. But the problem is that it needs to be coherent across all the possible intensity fields the model can generate, and that requires the types of considerations I described in my previous email, so it’s likely not a usable approach.

Finn
